statement: Every finite-dimensional [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra) $\mathfrak g$ over a field of characteristic zero has a [semisimple](c:is-semisimple) subalgebra $\mathfrak s$ with $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak r\oplus\mathfrak s$ as vector spaces, where $\mathfrak r$ is the [solvable radical](c:solvable-radical) of $\mathfrak g$.

hypotheses.text: The [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra) $\mathfrak g$ has finite dimension over a field $k$.
The field $k$ has characteristic zero.

conclusion: There is a [semisimple](c:is-semisimple) subalgebra $\mathfrak s$ with $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak r\oplus\mathfrak s$, so $\mathfrak g\cong\mathfrak r\rtimes\mathfrak s$ is a [semidirect product](c:semidirect-product-lie-algebra).

proofs.name: Whitehead's lemma and induction
proofs.slogan: Split off the radical by induction, and kill the obstruction in the abelian case with Whitehead's second lemma.
proofs.scope: All finite-dimensional $\mathfrak g$ over a field of characteristic zero, by induction on $\dim\mathfrak g$. If $\mathfrak r=0$, then $\mathfrak g$ is semisimple and $\mathfrak s=\mathfrak g$; Whitehead's second lemma is used as a known result.

roles.why: Induction runs on the dimension, and Whitehead's lemma needs finite-dimensional modules.
Characteristic zero gives the vanishing of $H^2$ for modules of semisimple algebras.

steps.slogan: Reduce to an abelian radical by induction on the dimension.
steps.detail: Assume $\mathfrak r$ is not abelian. Then $I=[\mathfrak r,\mathfrak r]$ is a nonzero ideal of $\mathfrak g$, and $I\ne\mathfrak r$ because $\mathfrak r$ is [solvable](c:solvable-lie-algebra). Induction gives a complement $T/I$ of $\mathfrak r/I$ in $\mathfrak g/I$. The algebra $T$ has radical $I$ and $\dim T<\dim\mathfrak g$, so $T=I\oplus\mathfrak s$ and $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak r\oplus\mathfrak s$.

steps.slogan: Make the abelian radical a module over the semisimple quotient.
steps.detail: Let $\mathfrak r$ be abelian and $\bar{\mathfrak s}=\mathfrak g/\mathfrak r$, which is [semisimple](c:is-semisimple). Because $[\mathfrak r,\mathfrak r]=0$, the adjoint action of $\mathfrak g$ on $\mathfrak r$ factors through $\bar{\mathfrak s}$. So $\mathfrak r$ is a [module](c:lie-module) over $\bar{\mathfrak s}$, and $0\to\mathfrak r\to\mathfrak g\to\bar{\mathfrak s}\to0$ is an [extension](c:is-extension).

steps.slogan: Measure the failure of a linear section to be a homomorphism.
steps.detail: Pick a linear map $\sigma\colon\bar{\mathfrak s}\to\mathfrak g$ with $\pi\sigma=\mathrm{id}$, and put $c(x,y)=[\sigma x,\sigma y]-\sigma[x,y]$. It takes values in $\mathfrak r$. The Jacobi identity makes $c$ a 2-cocycle, a cochain of the [Lie algebra cohomology](c:lie-algebra-cohomology) of $\bar{\mathfrak s}$ with values in $\mathfrak r$.

steps.slogan: Kill the cocycle with Whitehead's second lemma.
steps.detail: Whitehead's second lemma says $H^2(\bar{\mathfrak s},M)=0$ for every finite-dimensional module $M$ of a semisimple Lie algebra in characteristic zero. So there is a linear $\beta\colon\bar{\mathfrak s}\to\mathfrak r$ with $c(x,y)=-\big(x\cdot\beta(y)-y\cdot\beta(x)-\beta([x,y])\big)$.

steps.slogan: Correct the section by $ eta$ to get a Lie homomorphism.
steps.detail: Put $\sigma'=\sigma+\beta$. Since $\mathfrak r$ is abelian, $[\sigma'x,\sigma'y]-\sigma'[x,y]=c(x,y)+x\cdot\beta(y)-y\cdot\beta(x)-\beta([x,y])=0$. So $\sigma'$ is a [Lie algebra homomorphism](c:lie-hom) with $\pi\sigma'=\mathrm{id}$.

steps.slogan: Take the image of the homomorphism as the Levi subalgebra.
steps.detail: The image $\mathfrak s=\sigma'(\bar{\mathfrak s})$ is a subalgebra isomorphic to $\mathfrak g/\mathfrak r$, so it is semisimple. It meets $\mathfrak r$ only in $0$ and has complementary dimension. So $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak r\oplus\mathfrak s$, and $\mathfrak g\cong\mathfrak r\rtimes\mathfrak s$.

concepts.c:lie-algebra: The theorem is about finite-dimensional Lie algebras and their subalgebras.
concepts.c:is-semisimple: The complement is semisimple, and the quotient by the radical is semisimple.
concepts.c:solvable-radical: The radical is the largest solvable ideal that the complement must avoid.
concepts.c:semidirect-product-lie-algebra: The splitting writes the algebra as the radical extended by the complement.
concepts.c:solvable-lie-algebra: A solvable radical is not equal to its derived algebra unless it is zero.
concepts.c:lie-module: The abelian radical becomes a module over the semisimple quotient.
concepts.c:is-extension: The algebra is an extension of the quotient by the radical.
concepts.c:lie-algebra-cohomology: The obstruction to a splitting is a class in second cohomology.
concepts.c:lie-hom: A section that is a homomorphism has an image that is a subalgebra.

source.note: The classical proof by induction and Whitehead's second lemma, as in Jacobson, Lie Algebras, Chapter III, and Humphreys, Introduction to Lie Algebras and Representation Theory, Chapter VI (Humphreys uses a different route through Weyl's theorem).

statement: Every closed, orientable, connected [3-manifold](c:3-manifold) is obtained by [Dehn surgery](c:dehn-surgery) on a [framed link](c:framed-link) in $S^3$ whose surgery coefficients are all $\pm1$. The components of the link can be taken [unknotted](c:unknot).

hypotheses.text: The 3-manifold $M$ is [closed](c:closed-manifold): compact and without boundary.
The manifold $M$ is orientable.
The manifold $M$ is connected.

conclusion: There is a link in $S^3$ with unknotted components and framings $\pm1$ whose [Dehn surgery](c:dehn-surgery) gives a manifold homeomorphic to $M$.

proofs.name: Heegaard splitting and Dehn twists
proofs.slogan: Cut the manifold along a Heegaard surface, write the regluing map as Dehn twists, and turn each twist into a surgery.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, in the PL or smooth category; the proof is an outline that rests on Lickorish's paper. The manifold is compared with $S^3$ through one Heegaard surface of genus $g$.

roles.why: Compactness gives a finite triangulation, hence a Heegaard splitting of finite genus.
An orientation makes the regluing map orientation preserving, so Dehn twists generate it.
A connected manifold has a Heegaard splitting along one connected surface.

steps.slogan: Split the manifold along a Heegaard surface into two handlebodies.
steps.detail: Triangulate $M$ by Moise's theorem. A regular neighborhood of the 1-skeleton is a [handlebody](c:handlebody) $H$, and the closure of its complement is a handlebody of the same genus $g$. This is a [Heegaard splitting](c:heegaard-splitting).

steps.slogan: Compare the manifold with the sphere by a regluing map of the surface.
steps.detail: The sphere $S^3$ has a standard Heegaard splitting of every genus $g$. Hence $M$ is obtained from $S^3$ by cutting along the surface $\Sigma_g$ and regluing by an orientation-preserving homeomorphism $\varphi$ of $\Sigma_g$.

steps.slogan: Write the regluing map as a product of Dehn twists.
steps.detail: By the Lickorish twist theorem, the [mapping class group](c:mapping-class-group) of $\Sigma_g$ is generated by [Dehn twists](c:dehn-twist) about finitely many fixed curves. So $\varphi$ is isotopic to a product $\tau_{c_1}^{\pm1}\cdots\tau_{c_k}^{\pm1}$ of such twists.

steps.slogan: Replace each twist by surgery on its curve pushed into a collar.
steps.detail: Cutting along a collar of $\Sigma_g$ and regluing by $\tau_c^{\pm1}$ gives the same manifold as surgery on the curve $c$, pushed into the collar, with coefficient $\pm1$ relative to the framing that the surface induces.

steps.slogan: Stack the pushed curves at different levels to form one framed link.
steps.detail: Push $c_1,\dots,c_k$ to distinct levels of a collar $\Sigma_g\times[0,1]\subset S^3$. The generating curves can be chosen unknotted in $S^3$ with surface framing $0$, so the result is a link with unknotted components and coefficients $\pm1$.

steps.slogan: Read the surgered sphere as the manifold $M$.
steps.detail: Surgery on this link gives $S^3$ cut along $\Sigma_g$ and reglued by $\varphi$, which is $M$. All coefficients are $\pm1$ and all components are unknotted.

concepts.c:3-manifold: The theorem describes every closed orientable 3-manifold through one construction.
concepts.c:dehn-surgery: Surgery on the link realizes the regluing of the Heegaard surface.
concepts.c:framed-link: The surgery data are a link with an integer framing on each component.
concepts.c:unknot: Each surgery curve is unknotted in the sphere.
concepts.c:closed-manifold: Compactness without boundary gives a finite Heegaard splitting.
concepts.c:handlebody: The two sides of a Heegaard splitting are handlebodies.
concepts.c:heegaard-splitting: The splitting turns a 3-manifold into a gluing map of a surface.
concepts.c:mapping-class-group: The regluing map is an element of the mapping class group.
concepts.c:dehn-twist: Dehn twists generate the mapping class group and become surgeries.

source.ref: W. B. R. Lickorish, A representation of orientable combinatorial 3-manifolds, Annals of Mathematics 76 (1962), 531-540
source.note: Lickorish's proof: Heegaard splitting, generation of the homeotopy group by twists, and the twist-to-surgery lemma.

statement: Let $f\colon N\to P$ be a [proper](c:proper-map) [smooth map](c:smooth-map) between smooth manifolds. Then $f$ is [stable](c:stable-map) if and only if $f$ is [infinitesimally stable](c:infinitesimal-stability).

hypotheses.text: $N$ and $P$ are [smooth manifolds](c:smooth-manifold), Hausdorff and second countable.
The map $f\colon N\to P$ is [smooth](c:smooth-map).
The map $f$ is [proper](c:proper-map): preimages of compact sets are compact.

conclusion: Every map near $f$ is equivalent to $f$ by diffeomorphisms of $N$ and $P$ exactly when every vector field along $f$ has the form $df(u)+v\circ f$ with $u$ on $N$ and $v$ on $P$.

proofs.name: Homotopy method and division theorem
proofs.slogan: Turn infinitesimal stability into a trivialization of nearby maps with the division theorem, and prove the converse separately.
proofs.scope: Both implications, for proper maps; the proof is an outline of Mather's work and rests on the cited papers. Mather's Part II proves that infinitesimal stability implies stability.

roles.why: Charts and partitions of unity let local solutions glue into global vector fields.
Smoothness makes vector fields along $f$ and the module structure over functions on $P$ meaningful.
Properness keeps the property open and controls the supports, so the flows of the fields exist.

steps.slogan: Join a nearby map to $f$ by a path and form the unfolding.
steps.detail: Let $g$ be close to $f$ and put $f_t=f+t(g-f)$ in charts. For proper maps infinitesimal stability is an open condition, so each $f_t$ with small $t$ is infinitesimally stable. It then suffices to find time-dependent vector fields $u_t$ on $N$ and $v_t$ on $P$ with $\partial_tf_t=df_t(u_t)+v_t\circ f_t$.

steps.slogan: Solve the infinitesimal equation near each point by the division theorem.
steps.detail: Locally the equation is a statement about modules of germs over the ring of germs on $P$. The Malgrange-Mather division theorem lets one pass from solvability modulo the maximal ideal to solvability of the equation for germs, by a Nakayama-type argument.

steps.slogan: Glue the local solutions into global vector fields with a partition of unity.
steps.detail: The equation is linear in $(u_t,v_t)$. So local solutions on a locally finite cover add up with a partition of unity, and they give smooth families $u_t$ on $N$ and $v_t$ on $P$ that solve the equation everywhere.

steps.slogan: Integrate the vector fields to get diffeomorphisms that conjugate $f_t$ to $f$.
steps.detail: Properness of $f$ controls the supports, so the flows $\xi_t$ on $N$ and $\eta_t$ on $P$ exist up to time $1$. They satisfy $f_t=\eta_t\circ f\circ\xi_t^{-1}$, so $g=f_1$ is equivalent to $f$. Thus an infinitesimally stable proper map is stable.

steps.slogan: Prove the converse: a stable map is infinitesimally stable.
steps.detail: This is the second half of Mather's theorem. It does not follow by differentiating, because the equivalences that stability gives need not depend smoothly on the parameter. The cited work proves it by a separate argument.

steps.slogan: Combine the two implications into the equivalence.
steps.detail: Infinitesimal stability implies stability by the homotopy method, and stability implies infinitesimal stability by the converse. So a proper smooth map is stable if and only if it is infinitesimally stable.

concepts.c:proper-map: Properness makes infinitesimal stability open and lets the vector fields integrate.
concepts.c:smooth-map: The map and its nearby maps are smooth, so vector fields along $f$ make sense.
concepts.c:stable-map: Stability is one side of the equivalence that the proof establishes.
concepts.c:infinitesimal-stability: Infinitesimal stability is the linear condition solved by the division theorem.
concepts.c:smooth-manifold: Smooth charts and partitions of unity glue the local solutions.

source.ref: J. N. Mather, Stability of C-infinity mappings. II. Infinitesimal stability implies stability, Annals of Mathematics 89 (1969), 254-291; with M. Golubitsky and V. Guillemin, Stable Mappings and Their Singularities, Graduate Texts in Mathematics 14, Springer, 1973
source.note: Mather's Part II proves that infinitesimal stability implies stability; the Golubitsky-Guillemin book gives an account of both implications.

statement: Let $E$ be a complex Banach space and $f\colon\mathbb C\to E$ a function that is [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) on all of $\mathbb C$. Then $f$ has a [primitive](c:antiderivative): a function $F$ with $F'(z)=f(z)$ for every $z$.

hypotheses.text: The function $f\colon\mathbb C\to E$ is [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) on $\mathbb C$.
The space $E$ is a complex [Banach space](c:banach-space).

conclusion: There is a [primitive](c:antiderivative) $F\colon\mathbb C\to E$ with $F'(z)=f(z)$ for all $z\in\mathbb C$.

formal.difference: The declaration says IsExactOn f univ, that is, some g has HasDerivAt g (f z) z for every z, for f differentiable on the plane with values in a complete complex normed space. The converse of Morera (a continuous f with zero rectangle integrals is holomorphic) is the separate lemma isConservativeOn_and_continuousOn_iff_isDifferentiableOn.

proofs.name: Wedge integral primitive
proofs.slogan: Integrate along a horizontal and then a vertical segment from zero, and use Goursat to show that the derivative is $f$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, for any complex Banach space $E$, so $E=\mathbb C$ is included. The path is a horizontal segment followed by a vertical segment, so no general path integral is needed.

roles.why: Holomorphy gives continuity of $f$ and the vanishing rectangle integrals.
Completeness of $E$ makes the integrals along the segments exist.

steps.slogan: Show that every rectangle integral of $f$ vanishes.
steps.detail: The function $f$ is [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) on every rectangle, so the Cauchy-Goursat theorem for rectangles gives $\oint_{\partial R}f=0$ for each rectangle $R$. In wedge notation, the wedge from $z$ to $w$ equals minus the wedge from $w$ to $z$.

steps.slogan: Define the candidate primitive by the wedge integral from zero.
steps.detail: For $z=x+iy$ put $F(z)=\int_0^xf(t)\,dt+i\int_0^yf(x+is)\,ds$. This is a horizontal segment from $0$ to $x$ and then a vertical segment up to $z$. Both integrals exist because $f$ is continuous and $E$ is complete.

steps.slogan: Compare the wedge from zero with the wedge from a nearby point.
steps.detail: For $w$ near $z$, the wedges $0\to z$, $z\to w$ and $0\to w$ differ by integrals over rectangles in a disc around $0$. By step 1 those integrals vanish, so $F(w)-F(z)$ equals the wedge integral of $f$ from $z$ to $w$.

steps.slogan: Differentiate the wedge integral from $z$ to $w$ by continuity of $f$.
steps.detail: The wedge from $z$ to $w$ has a horizontal and a vertical part. By continuity, each part equals $f(z)$ times its complex length plus $o(|w-z|)$. So $F(w)-F(z)=f(z)(w-z)+o(|w-z|)$, and the [complex derivative](c:complex-derivative) of $F$ at every $z$ is $f(z)$.

concepts.c:holomorphic-function: Holomorphy of $f$ gives the vanishing rectangle integrals and continuity.
concepts.c:banach-space: Completeness of the value space makes the segment integrals exist.
concepts.c:antiderivative: The wedge integral is the primitive that the theorem promises.
concepts.c:complex-derivative: The primitive is shown complex differentiable with derivative $f$.

source.note: mathlib takes the primitive Complex.wedgeIntegral 0 z f, with DifferentiableOn.isConservativeOn (Goursat) and IsConservativeOn.hasDerivAt_wedgeIntegral.

statement: Let $M$ and $N$ be nonempty [smooth manifolds](c:smooth-manifold) of dimensions $m\ne n$. Then no continuous map $M\to N$ is a bijection.

hypotheses.text: $M$ and $N$ are nonempty [smooth manifolds](c:smooth-manifold), Hausdorff and second countable.
The [dimensions](c:manifold-dimension) differ: $\dim M=m\ne n=\dim N$.

conclusion: No continuous map $f\colon M\to N$ is a bijection.

proofs.name: Invariance of domain and Baire category
proofs.slogan: Assume a continuous bijection, embed an open piece of the higher-dimensional manifold into the lower-dimensional one, and contradict invariance of domain.
proofs.scope: Dimension $0$ is included, since $\mathbb R^0$ is a point. The proof works for topological manifolds, and it splits into the cases $m>n$ and $m<n$.

roles.why: Second countability gives sigma-compactness, and local compactness makes $N$ a Baire space.
The dimensions differ, so one case applies and the lemma contradicts the embedding.

steps.slogan: Show that no open subset of $\mathbb R^p$ maps continuously and injectively into $\mathbb R^q$ for $q<p$.
steps.detail: Suppose $h\colon V\to\mathbb R^q$ is continuous and injective on a nonempty open $V\subset\mathbb R^p$. Compose $h$ with the inclusion $y\mapsto(y,0)$ of $\mathbb R^q$ in $\mathbb R^p$. By Brouwer's invariance of domain the image is open in $\mathbb R^p$, but it lies in $\mathbb R^q\times\{0\}$, which has empty interior.

steps.slogan: Treat the case $m>n$ by mapping a coordinate ball of $M$ into a chart of $N$.
steps.detail: Take $x_0\in M$ and a chart $\varphi\colon W\to\mathbb R^n$ of $N$ at $f(x_0)$. By continuity, a small coordinate ball $V\subset\mathbb R^m$ around $x_0$ has $f(V)\subset W$. Then $\varphi\circ f|_V$ is continuous and injective into $\mathbb R^n$ with $n<m$, against step 1.

steps.slogan: Treat the case $m<n$ by writing $M$ as a countable union of compact sets.
steps.detail: A second countable, locally compact Hausdorff space is [sigma-compact](c:sigma-compact-space), so $M=\bigcup K_i$ with $K_i$ [compact](c:compact-space). Each $f(K_i)$ is compact, hence closed in the [Hausdorff space](c:hausdorff-space) $N$, and $N=\bigcup f(K_i)$ because $f$ is onto.

steps.slogan: Find one image $f(K_i)$ with interior and invert $f$ on $K_i$.
steps.detail: A locally compact Hausdorff space is a [Baire space](c:baire-space), so some $f(K_i)$ has nonempty interior $U$. The map $f|_{K_i}\colon K_i\to f(K_i)$ is a continuous bijection from a compact space onto a Hausdorff space, so it is a [homeomorphism](c:homeomorphism). Call its inverse $g$.

steps.slogan: Embed a small open piece of $N$ into a chart of $M$ by $g$.
steps.detail: Take $y_0\in U$, a chart $\varphi$ of $N$ near $y_0$ inside $U$, and a chart $\psi$ of $M$ at $g(y_0)$. By continuity of $g$, a smaller ball $B\subset\mathbb R^n$ has $\psi\circ g\circ\varphi^{-1}$ defined, continuous and injective into $\mathbb R^m$ with $m<n$. This contradicts step 1.

steps.slogan: Combine the two cases to exclude every continuous bijection.
steps.detail: Because $m\ne n$, either $m>n$ or $m<n$. Each case gives a contradiction, so no continuous bijection $M\to N$ exists.

concepts.c:smooth-manifold: Manifolds are locally Euclidean, second countable and Hausdorff, which the proof uses.
concepts.c:manifold-dimension: The two dimensions differ, which splits the proof into two cases.
concepts.c:sigma-compact-space: A countable union of compact sets covers the domain.
concepts.c:compact-space: Compact sets have compact, hence closed, images.
concepts.c:hausdorff-space: Compact subsets of a Hausdorff space are closed.
concepts.c:baire-space: Baire category gives one image set with nonempty interior.
concepts.c:homeomorphism: A bijection from a compact set to a Hausdorff space has a continuous inverse.

source.note: The standard argument from Brouwer's invariance of domain and the Baire category theorem; it is not a mathlib proof.

statement: A finite graph $G$ is [perfect](c:perfect-graph) if and only if its complement $\overline G$ is perfect. Here perfect means that $\chi(H)=\omega(H)$ for every [induced subgraph](c:induced-subgraph) $H$.

hypotheses.text: $G$ is a finite simple undirected graph.

conclusion: The graph $G$ is [perfect](c:perfect-graph) exactly when $\overline G$ is perfect.

proofs.name: Lovász replication
proofs.slogan: Replicate vertices to show that a perfect graph has a clique meeting every maximum independent set, then remove that clique by induction.
proofs.scope: One direction by induction on the number of vertices: if $G$ is perfect, then $\overline G$ is perfect. The converse follows by applying this to $\overline G$, because $\overline{\overline G}=G$.

roles.why: Finiteness gives finitely many maximum independent sets and lets induction on the number of vertices run.

steps.slogan: Show that replacing a vertex of a perfect graph by two adjacent twins keeps it perfect.
steps.detail: Let $v'$ be adjacent to $v$ and to every neighbor of $v$, and let $k=\omega(G)$. If $v$ lies in a $k$-clique, give $v'$ a new color. Otherwise take a $k$-coloring, let $S$ be the class of $v$ and $S'=S\setminus\{v\}$. Then $G-S'$ has no $k$-clique, so $k-1$ colors suffice for it, and $S'\cup\{v'\}$ is the last class.

steps.slogan: Replace each vertex by a clique whose size counts the maximum independent sets through it.
steps.detail: Let $S_1,\dots,S_r$ be the [maximum independent sets](c:is-maximum-indep-set) of $G$, of size $\alpha$. Replace each vertex $v$ by a clique of size $w(v)=\#\{i:v\in S_i\}$, and delete $v$ if $w(v)=0$. By step 1 the new graph $G'$ is perfect.

steps.slogan: Count the vertices of the new graph to find a clique that meets every maximum independent set.
steps.detail: Suppose no [clique](c:clique) $Q$ of $G$ meets all $S_i$. Then each $Q$ misses some $S_j$ and meets the others in at most one vertex, so $w(Q)\le r-1$ and $\omega(G')\le r-1$. Also $|V(G')|=r\alpha$ and $\alpha(G')\le\alpha$. A perfect graph has $|V|\le\alpha\omega$, so $r\alpha\le\alpha(r-1)$, which is false.

steps.slogan: Delete that clique to lower the independence number by one.
steps.detail: Let $Q$ be a clique that meets every maximum [independent set](c:independent-set). Then no independent set of size $\alpha$ avoids $Q$, and a maximum independent set loses one vertex in $G-Q$. So $\alpha(G-Q)=\alpha-1$, and $G-Q$ is perfect with fewer vertices.

steps.slogan: Cover $G-Q$ by cliques with the induction hypothesis, then add $Q$.
steps.detail: By induction on the number of vertices, $\overline{G-Q}$ is perfect, so its [chromatic number](c:chromatic-number) is $\omega(\overline{G-Q})=\alpha-1$. So $G-Q$ is covered by $\alpha-1$ cliques. With $Q$ these are $\alpha$ cliques that cover $G$, so $\chi(\overline G)\le\alpha(G)=\omega(\overline G)$, and equality holds.

steps.slogan: Check that every induced subgraph of the complement also has equal coloring and clique numbers.
steps.detail: An induced subgraph of $\overline G$ is the complement $\overline H$ of an induced subgraph $H$ of $G$. The graph $H$ is perfect, so for $H\ne G$ induction gives $\chi(\overline H)=\omega(\overline H)$. Step 5 gives it for $H=G$. So $\overline G$ is perfect.

concepts.c:perfect-graph: The theorem says that perfection passes to the complement graph.
concepts.c:induced-subgraph: Perfection is a condition on every induced subgraph, and induction passes to them.
concepts.c:is-maximum-indep-set: The weights count the maximum independent sets through each vertex.
concepts.c:clique: A clique through the maximum independent sets is the object that the proof finds.
concepts.c:independent-set: Independent sets of the graph become cliques of the complement.
concepts.c:chromatic-number: The complement's chromatic number is the minimum number of cliques that cover.

source.note: Lovász's replication proof (Normal hypergraphs and the perfect graph conjecture, Discrete Mathematics 2 (1972), 253-267), as presented in Diestel, Graph Theory, section 5.5.

statement: Let $(M_n)$ be a positive [log-convex](c:log-convex-sequence) sequence with $M_0=1$. The class of [smooth functions](c:smooth-function) $f$ on $\mathbb R$ with $\sup|f^{(n)}|\le\beta B^nM_n$, where $\beta,B$ depend on $f$, is quasi-analytic if and only if $\sum_{n\ge1}M_{n-1}/M_n=\infty$. Quasi-analytic means that a function of the class vanishes when its [Taylor series](c:taylor-series) at one point is zero.

hypotheses.text: $(M_n)_{n\ge0}$ is a sequence of positive numbers with $M_0=1$.
The sequence is [log-convex](c:log-convex-sequence): $M_n^2\le M_{n-1}M_{n+1}$ for all $n\ge1$.

conclusion: The class is quasi-analytic exactly when $\sum_{n\ge1}M_{n-1}/M_n$ diverges.

proofs.name: Fourier transform and Carleman's inequality
proofs.slogan: Turn the series into a logarithmic integral, then link the integral to flat functions of the class through Fourier and Laplace transforms.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem on the real line; the proof is an outline of Rudin's account and rests on the cited book. Carleman's form with $\sum M_n^{-1/n}$ is the first equivalence of the outline.

roles.why: Positivity and $M_0=1$ normalize the sequence and make $q(x)=\sup_n x^n/M_n$ well defined.
Log-convexity makes the ratios $M_{n-1}/M_n$ decrease, so Carleman's inequality gives an equivalence of series.

steps.slogan: Compare the series $\sum M_{n-1}/M_n$ and $\sum M_n^{-1/n}$ by Carleman's inequality.
steps.detail: Put $a_n=M_{n-1}/M_n$, so $(a_1\cdots a_n)^{1/n}=M_n^{-1/n}$. Carleman's inequality gives $\sum M_n^{-1/n}\le e\sum a_n$. Log-convexity makes $a_n$ decrease, so $a_n\le M_n^{-1/n}$. Hence the two series converge or diverge together.

steps.slogan: Replace the series by the integral of $\log q(x)/(1+x^2)$.
steps.detail: Put $q(x)=\sup_nx^n/M_n$ for $x>0$. For a log-convex sequence, $\int_1^\infty\log q(x)\,dx/(1+x^2)$ is finite exactly when $\sum M_n^{-1/n}$ is finite. This turns the question into a statement about a decay rate.

steps.slogan: Build a nonzero flat function of the class when the integral is finite.
steps.detail: A finite integral gives a nonzero bounded holomorphic function $F$ in the upper half-plane with $|F|$ of size $1/q$ on a horizontal line. Its inverse [Fourier transform](c:fourier-transform) is supported on $[0,\infty)$ by the Paley-Wiener theorem, and the decay gives $\sup|f^{(n)}|\le\beta B^nM_n$. So all derivatives of $f\ne0$ vanish at $0$.

steps.slogan: Show that a nonzero flat function of the class forces the integral to be finite.
steps.detail: Let $f\ne0$ be in the class with all derivatives zero at $0$, and put $F(z)=\int_0^\infty f(t)e^{izt}dt$ for $\operatorname{Im}z>0$. Integration by parts $n$ times gives $|F(z)|\le\beta B^nM_n/(|z|^n\operatorname{Im}z)$, so $|F|\lesssim1/q$. A nonzero bounded holomorphic function has a logarithm that is integrable against $dt/(1+t^2)$, by Jensen's formula, so the integral is finite.

steps.slogan: Chain the equivalences to get the Denjoy-Carleman criterion.
steps.detail: The class is not quasi-analytic exactly when the integral is finite (steps 3 and 4). The integral is finite exactly when $\sum M_{n-1}/M_n$ is finite (steps 1 and 2). So the class is quasi-analytic exactly when $\sum M_{n-1}/M_n$ diverges.

concepts.c:log-convex-sequence: Log-convexity makes the ratios monotone and lets $q$ recover the sequence.
concepts.c:smooth-function: The class consists of smooth functions with controlled derivatives.
concepts.c:taylor-series: Quasi-analyticity says that the Taylor series at a point fixes the function.
concepts.c:fourier-transform: The transform turns decay of $F$ into derivative bounds on $f$.

source.ref: W. Rudin, Real and Complex Analysis, 3rd edition, McGraw-Hill, 1987, Theorem 19.11 (the Denjoy-Carleman theorem)
source.note: Rudin's proof of the Denjoy-Carleman theorem, through Carleman's inequality, the function q, the Paley-Wiener theorem and Jensen's formula.

statement: Let $f=p\circ i$ in a category, with $i\colon A\to X$ and $p\colon X\to B$. If $f$ has the [left lifting property](c:has-lifting-property) against $p$, then $f$ is a [retract](c:retract) of $i$ in the [arrow category](c:arrow-category).

hypotheses.text: The morphism $f\colon A\to B$ factors as $f=p\circ i$ with $i\colon A\to X$ and $p\colon X\to B$.
The morphism $f$ has the [left lifting property](c:has-lifting-property) against $p$.

conclusion: There are morphisms $f\to i$ and $i\to f$ of the [arrow category](c:arrow-category) whose composite is the identity of $f$, so $f$ is a [retract](c:retract) of $i$.

proofs.name: Lift in the factorization square
proofs.slogan: Lift in the square formed by the factorization and the identity of $B$, then read off the two maps of the retract.
proofs.scope: The left lifting case. The dual case, where $f$ has the right lifting property against $i$ and $f$ is a retract of $p$, follows by reversing all arrows.

roles.why: The factorization supplies the commutative square and the maps $i$ and $p$ of the retract diagram.
Lifting against $p$ gives the diagonal map $B\to X$.

steps.slogan: Form the square with $f$ on the left, $p$ on the right and top $i$.
steps.detail: The square has left side $f\colon A\to B$, right side $p\colon X\to B$, top $i\colon A\to X$ and bottom $\mathrm{id}_B$. This [commutative diagram](c:commutative-diagram) commutes because $p\circ i=f=\mathrm{id}_B\circ f$.

steps.slogan: Take the diagonal filler that the lifting property gives.
steps.detail: Since $f$ has the [lifting property](c:has-lifting-property) against $p$, there is $h\colon B\to X$ with $h\circ f=i$ and $p\circ h=\mathrm{id}_B$.

steps.slogan: Write the two morphisms between $f$ and $i$ in the arrow category.
steps.detail: The pair $(\mathrm{id}_A,h)$ is a morphism $f\to i$, because $h\circ f=i\circ\mathrm{id}_A$. The pair $(\mathrm{id}_A,p)$ is a morphism $i\to f$, because $p\circ i=f\circ\mathrm{id}_A$.

steps.slogan: Check that the composite of the two morphisms is the identity of $f$.
steps.detail: The composite $f\to i\to f$ is $(\mathrm{id}_A,p\circ h)=(\mathrm{id}_A,\mathrm{id}_B)$. So $f$ is a retract of $i$. In a [weak factorization system](c:weak-factorization-system), a map with the left lifting property against the right class is therefore a retract of the left factor of its factorization.

concepts.c:has-lifting-property: The lifting property supplies the diagonal map of the retract.
concepts.c:retract: The conclusion says that $f$ is a retract of $i$.
concepts.c:arrow-category: The retract is a retract of objects in the arrow category.
concepts.c:commutative-diagram: The factorization gives a commuting square to lift in.
concepts.c:weak-factorization-system: The argument shows that left classes of such systems are closed under retracts.

source.note: The standard retract argument, as on the nLab page retract argument and in Hovey, Model Categories, section 1.1.

statement: Let $I$ be an interval and $f\colon I\to I$ a [continuous function](c:continuous-function). Order the positive integers by $3\prec5\prec7\prec\cdots\prec2\cdot3\prec2\cdot5\prec\cdots\prec2^2\cdot3\prec\cdots\prec2^3\prec2^2\prec2\prec1$. If $f$ has a [periodic point](c:periodic-point) of least period $m$ and $m\prec n$, then $f$ has a periodic point of least period $n$.

hypotheses.text: The set $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is an [interval](c:interval).
The map $f\colon I\to I$ is [continuous](c:continuous-function).
The map $f$ has a [periodic point](c:periodic-point) of least period $m$.
The integer $n$ comes after $m$ in the Sharkovskii order: $m\prec n$.

conclusion: The map $f$ has a periodic point of least period $n$.

proofs.name: Interval loops and Markov graph
proofs.slogan: Turn a periodic orbit into loops of covering intervals, count the loop lengths, and treat odd, doubled and power-of-two periods in turn.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, as an outline of the Burns-Hasselblatt proof, which rests on the cited paper. A closed bounded interval suffices, because the orbit lies in one.

roles.why: Intervals are connected, so the intermediate value theorem turns covering into periodic points.
Continuity gives the covering property of images of intervals.
The orbit of the periodic point supplies the intervals of the Markov graph.
The position of $n$ after $m$ decides which of the three cases produces $n$.

steps.slogan: Show that a loop of covering intervals contains a periodic point.
steps.detail: Write $J_0\to J_1$ if $f(J_0)\supseteq J_1$ for closed intervals. For a loop $J_0\to\cdots\to J_{n-1}\to J_0$, the intermediate value theorem gives $x\in J_0$ with $f^k(x)\in J_k$ and $f^n(x)=x$. If the loop is not a repetition of a shorter loop, $x$ can be chosen with least period $n$, after a separate treatment of endpoints.

steps.slogan: Read the covering relations of the periodic orbit from its Markov graph.
steps.detail: Order the orbit points $p_1<\dots<p_m$ and let $J_i=[p_i,p_{i+1}]$. Since $f$ permutes the points, $f(J_i)$ covers each $J_j$ between the images of $p_i$ and $p_{i+1}$. These relations form a directed graph, and its loops give periodic points by step 1.

steps.slogan: Show that a least odd period $m>1$ gives loops of every needed length.
steps.detail: Let $m>1$ be the least odd period of $f$. A periodic orbit of that period then has the Štefan structure, and its graph has loops of length $1$, of every even length below $m$ and of every length at least $m$. So $f$ has points of all those least periods.

steps.slogan: Treat periods $2^km$ with $m$ odd by passing to the iterate $f^{2^k}$.
steps.detail: If $f$ has least period $2^km$ with $m>1$ odd, then $f^{2^k}$ has a point of least period $m$. Apply step 3 to $f^{2^k}$ and keep track of how $f$ permutes the $2^k$ pieces of the orbit. This turns the periods of the iterate into the periods $2^kn$ for odd $n>m$ and the larger doubled periods.

steps.slogan: Treat least periods $2^k$ by descending through the powers of two.
steps.detail: A period-$2$ orbit $\{a,b\}$ gives a [fixed point](c:fixed-point) by the intermediate value theorem on $[a,b]$. For $k\ge2$, pass to $f^2$, which has least period $2^{k-1}$, and use induction to get all $2^j$ with $j<k$. No odd period is needed.

steps.slogan: Match the position of $n$ after $m$ with the case that produces it.
steps.detail: For odd $m$, step 3 gives every $n\succ m$. For $m=2^km'$ with $m'>1$ odd, step 4 gives every $n\succ m$. For $m=2^k$, step 5 gives all smaller powers of two and the fixed point, which are the $n\succ m$.

concepts.c:interval: The orbit and its Markov intervals live in an interval of the line.
concepts.c:continuous-function: Continuity makes the image of an interval an interval, which gives covering.
concepts.c:periodic-point: Periodic points are produced from loops of intervals.
concepts.c:fixed-point: The base case of the powers of two is a fixed point.

source.ref: K. Burns and B. Hasselblatt, The Sharkovsky theorem: a natural direct proof, American Mathematical Monthly 118 (2011), 229-244
source.note: A short published proof of the full theorem; the steps follow its loops of intervals, Štefan cycles and period doubling.

statement: Let $p,q\in\mathbb C$, let $s^2=q^2/4+p^3/27$ with $A=-q/2+s\ne0$, let $u$ be a [cube root](c:cube-root) of $A$, and put $v=-p/(3u)$ and $\omega=e^{2\pi i/3}$. Then the [roots](c:root-of-a-polynomial) of $x^3+px+q$ are $u+v$, $\omega u+\omega^2v$ and $\omega^2u+\omega v$. A general cubic $ax^3+bx^2+cx+d$ reduces to this form by $x=y-b/(3a)$.

hypotheses.text: The numbers $p$ and $q$ are [complex numbers](c:complex-number).
The number $s$ satisfies $s^2=q^2/4+p^3/27$, and $A=-q/2+s$ is nonzero.

conclusion: The identity $x^3+px+q=(x-u-v)(x-\omega u-\omega^2v)(x-\omega^2u-\omega v)$ holds, so these three numbers are the roots with multiplicity.

proofs.name: Cardano's substitution
proofs.slogan: Write the root as a sum of two cube roots, fix their product and the sum of their cubes, and factor the cubic with a cube identity.
proofs.scope: Complex roots of the depressed cubic; the general cubic reduces to it by a shift. If $p=q=0$, the cubic is $x^3$ and its only root is $0$; a sign of $s$ with $A\ne0$ exists in every other case.

roles.why: Complex numbers contain cube roots and the primitive cube root of unity $\omega$.
The condition on $s$ and $A\ne0$ makes $v$ defined and fixes the cubes $u^3$ and $v^3$.

steps.slogan: Remove the quadratic term of a general cubic by a shift.
steps.detail: For the [cubic](c:cubic) $ax^3+bx^2+cx+d$ with $a\ne0$, put $x=y-b/(3a)$ and divide by $a$. The result is $y^3+py+q$ with $p=(3ac-b^2)/(3a^2)$ and $q=(2b^3-9abc+27a^2d)/(27a^3)$.

steps.slogan: Compute $u^3$ and $v^3$ and show that $uv=-p/3$ and $u^3+v^3=-q$.
steps.detail: By definition $uv=-p/3$ and $u^3=A=-q/2+s$. Then $v^3=-p^3/(27A)$. Since $A(-q/2-s)=q^2/4-s^2=-p^3/27$, we get $v^3=-q/2-s$. Hence $u^3+v^3=-q$.

steps.slogan: State the cube identity that factors $x^3-3uvx-u^3-v^3$ into three linear factors.
steps.detail: For all complex $x,u,v$, $x^3-3uvx-u^3-v^3=(x-u-v)(x-\omega u-\omega^2v)(x-\omega^2u-\omega v)$. This is the factorization of $a^3+b^3+c^3-3abc$ with $a=x$, $b=-u$, $c=-v$. It uses $1+\omega+\omega^2=0$ and $\omega^3=1$.

steps.slogan: Insert the values from step 2 to factor the depressed cubic.
steps.detail: By step 2, $-3uv=p$ and $-(u^3+v^3)=q$. So $x^3+px+q=(x-u-v)(x-\omega u-\omega^2v)(x-\omega^2u-\omega v)$. The three numbers are the roots with multiplicity.

concepts.c:cube-root: The root is built from a cube root $u$ of $A$.
concepts.c:root-of-a-polynomial: The factorization lists all roots of the cubic with multiplicity.
concepts.c:complex-number: Complex numbers supply cube roots and the cube root of unity.
concepts.c:cubic: The general cubic is reduced to the depressed form first.

source.note: Cardano's formula (Ars Magna, 1545) derived through the factorization of a^3+b^3+c^3-3abc.

statement: Let a straight beam of constant flexural rigidity $EI$ rest on three level supports $A,B,C$ with spans $l=AB$ and $l'=BC$, under uniform downward loads $w$ and $w'$ per unit length. With sagging [bending moments](c:bending-moment) $M_A,M_B,M_C$ at the supports, $M_Al+2M_B(l+l')+M_Cl'=-\tfrac14\,(wl^3+w'l'^3)$.

hypotheses.text: The beam is straight, continuous over $B$ and of constant rigidity $EI$, and its deflection $y$ obeys $EI\,y''=-M$ with the [second derivative](c:second-derivative) $y''$.
The three supports $A,B,C$ are at the same level, so the deflection is zero at each of them.
The load is uniform: $w$ on $AB$ and $w'$ on $BC$.

proofs.name: Continuity of slope at the middle support
proofs.slogan: Integrate the beam law on each span, then equate the slopes of the two spans at $B$.
proofs.scope: Uniform loads and level supports; moments are positive when the beam sags, so support moments are usually negative. Other loads or settled supports add terms to the right side.

roles.why: The beam law links moments to curvature, and continuity over $B$ equates the slopes.
Zero deflection at both ends of each span fixes the end slopes.
Uniform loads give the parabolic part of the moment on each span.

steps.slogan: Write the bending moment on each span from statics.
steps.detail: On $AB$, with $x$ measured from $A$, the [bending moment](c:bending-moment) is $M(x)=M_A(1-x/l)+M_Bx/l+\tfrac12wx(l-x)$: the straight line through the end moments plus the simply supported parabola. On $BC$ the same holds with $M_B,M_C,w',l'$.

steps.slogan: Compute the slope at the right end of span $AB$.
steps.detail: Level supports give $y(0)=y(l)=0$, and $EI\,y''=-M$. Hence $y'(l)=\frac1l\int_0^lt\,y''(t)\,dt=-\frac1{EI\,l}\int_0^ltM(t)\,dt$, which equals $-\frac1{EI}\big(\tfrac{M_Al}6+\tfrac{M_Bl}3+\tfrac{wl^3}{24}\big)$.

steps.slogan: Compute the slope at the left end of span $BC$.
steps.detail: With $x$ measured from $B$, $y(0)=y(l')=0$ gives $y'(0)=-\frac1{l'}\int_0^{l'}(l'-t)\,y''(t)\,dt=\frac1{EI\,l'}\int_0^{l'}(l'-t)M(t)\,dt$. This equals $\frac1{EI}\big(\tfrac{M_Bl'}3+\tfrac{M_Cl'}6+\tfrac{w'l'^3}{24}\big)$.

steps.slogan: Equate the two slopes at $B$ because the beam is continuous there.
steps.detail: The deflection curve is smooth over $B$, so $y'(l^-)=y'(0^+)$. Hence $-\big(\tfrac{M_Al}6+\tfrac{M_Bl}3+\tfrac{wl^3}{24}\big)=\tfrac{M_Bl'}3+\tfrac{M_Cl'}6+\tfrac{w'l'^3}{24}$.

steps.slogan: Multiply by six and collect terms to get the three-moment equation.
steps.detail: Multiplying by $6$ gives $M_Al+2M_Bl+2M_Bl'+M_Cl'=-\tfrac14(wl^3+w'l'^3)$. The left side is $M_Al+2M_B(l+l')+M_Cl'$, which is the claim.

concepts.c:bending-moment: The bending moments at the supports are the unknowns of the equation.
concepts.c:second-derivative: The beam law ties the second derivative of the deflection to the moment.

source.note: The slope method of elementary beam theory, as in Timoshenko, Strength of Materials; the area-moment method gives the same equation.

new_concepts.name: bending moment
new_concepts.reminder: The bending moment at a beam section is the internal moment that resists bending there.
new_concepts.definition: The bending moment at a section of a beam is the sum of the moments, about the section, of the forces on one side of it. It is positive when the beam sags.

statement: Let $\alpha$ be a real [algebraic number](c:algebraic-number) that is irrational, and let $\varepsilon>0$. Then $|\alpha-p/q|<q^{-2-\varepsilon}$ has only finitely many solutions in integers $p$ and $q\ge1$.

hypotheses.text: The real number $\alpha$ is [algebraic](c:algebraic-number) and [irrational](c:irrational-number).
The exponent excess $\varepsilon$ is positive.

proofs.name: Roth's auxiliary polynomial
proofs.slogan: Assume infinitely many approximations, build an integer polynomial in many variables that vanishes to high order at the diagonal point, and compare a lower and an upper bound.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, as an outline of Roth's 1955 proof, which rests on the cited paper. Thue and Siegel proved weaker exponents by the same plan with one or two variables.

roles.why: Algebraicity of $\alpha$ gives the integer polynomial its vanishing at $(\alpha,\dots,\alpha)$ and keeps coefficients integral.
The excess $\varepsilon$ fixes how many variables are needed and makes the upper bound win.

steps.slogan: Assume infinitely many good approximations and pick $m$ of them with rapidly growing denominators.
steps.detail: Suppose $|\alpha-p/q|<q^{-2-\varepsilon}$ has infinitely many solutions. Fix $m$ large in terms of $\varepsilon$, and choose solutions $p_1/q_1,\dots,p_m/q_m$ with $q_1$ large and each $q_{j+1}$ much larger than a power of $q_j$.

steps.slogan: Build an integer polynomial in $m$ variables that vanishes to high order at the diagonal point.
steps.detail: Siegel's lemma, a pigeonhole count of unknowns against equations, gives a nonzero $P\in\mathbb Z[X_1,\dots,X_m]$ of degree at most $r_j$ in $X_j$, with the powers $q_j^{r_j}$ about equal and with small coefficients. All derivatives of small weighted index vanish at $(\alpha,\dots,\alpha)$.

steps.slogan: Show with Roth's lemma that a low-index derivative of $P$ does not vanish at the rational point.
steps.detail: Roth's lemma says that a nonzero integer polynomial of small height cannot vanish to high weighted index at $(p_1/q_1,\dots,p_m/q_m)$ when the $q_j$ grow fast enough. So some derivative $P_{(i)}$ of small index is nonzero there.

steps.slogan: Bound the nonzero derivative from below by its denominator.
steps.detail: The value $P_{(i)}(p_1/q_1,\dots,p_m/q_m)$ is a nonzero [rational number](c:rational-number) with denominator dividing $\prod q_j^{r_j}$. Hence its absolute value is at least $\prod q_j^{-r_j}$.

steps.slogan: Bound the same value from above by Taylor expansion and compare the two bounds.
steps.detail: Expand $P_{(i)}$ in a [Taylor series](c:taylor-series) around $(\alpha,\dots,\alpha)$. High-order vanishing and $|\alpha-p_j/q_j|<q_j^{-2-\varepsilon}$ make the value smaller than $\prod q_j^{-r_j}$ when $m$ is large. This contradicts step 4, so only finitely many approximations exist.

concepts.c:algebraic-number: Algebraicity of $\alpha$ lets one build the polynomial that vanishes at $\alpha$.
concepts.c:irrational-number: Irrationality rules out the trivial approximations by $\alpha$ itself.
concepts.c:rational-number: Rational points with large denominators carry the integrality lower bound.
concepts.c:taylor-series: Taylor expansion at the diagonal point gives the upper bound.

source.ref: K. F. Roth, Rational approximations to algebraic numbers, Mathematika 2 (1955), 1-20; corrigendum, 168
source.note: Roth's own proof: the auxiliary polynomial, Roth's lemma and the final comparison of bounds.

statement: Every [manifold](c:manifold) of dimension $2$ or $3$, Hausdorff and second countable, has a [triangulation](c:triangulation): it is homeomorphic to a locally finite simplicial complex.

hypotheses.text: $M$ is a Hausdorff, second countable topological [manifold](c:manifold).
The dimension of $M$ is $2$ or $3$.

conclusion: The manifold $M$ is homeomorphic to the underlying space of a locally finite [simplicial complex](c:simplicial-complex).

proofs.name: Radó and Moise
proofs.slogan: Triangulate coordinate balls one at a time and adjust the triangulations on the overlaps by small homeomorphisms until they fit.
proofs.scope: Dimensions $2$ (Radó, 1925) and $3$ (Moise, 1952), as an outline that rests on the cited work. The family also holds the failures: Freedman's $E_8$ manifold has no triangulation in dimension 4, and Manolescu showed that non-triangulable manifolds exist in every dimension from 5.

roles.why: Second countability gives a countable cover by coordinate balls and a locally finite union at the end.
Only dimensions 2 and 3 have the Schoenflies and tame-approximation tools that the steps use.

steps.slogan: Cover the manifold by countably many coordinate balls.
steps.detail: Since $M$ is second countable and locally Euclidean, it has a locally finite countable cover by coordinate balls $B_1,B_2,\dots$. The triangulation is built one ball at a time.

steps.slogan: In dimension 2 use the Schoenflies theorem to cut the surface into polygonal discs.
steps.detail: For a [surface](c:surface), Radó's proof uses the Jordan curve theorem and its strengthening, the Schoenflies theorem, to cut each coordinate ball into discs bounded by polygonal arcs. The pieces are then triangulated and fit along common boundary polygons.

steps.slogan: In dimension 3 approximate homeomorphisms by piecewise linear ones.
steps.detail: Moise's central tool, with Bing, is the approximation theorem: a homeomorphism between triangulated [3-manifolds](c:3-manifold) can be approximated by piecewise linear homeomorphisms. Its proof needs a long analysis of tame spheres and surfaces in 3-manifolds.

steps.slogan: Extend the triangulation ball by ball and adjust the overlaps by small homeomorphisms.
steps.detail: Assume the union $U_k$ of the first $k$ balls is triangulated. On the overlap with $B_{k+1}$, the coordinate homeomorphism is straightened (dimension 2) or approximated by a piecewise linear one (dimension 3). A small homeomorphism makes both triangulations agree there, so the triangulation extends over $U_{k+1}$.

steps.slogan: Take the union of the nested triangulated pieces to triangulate the manifold.
steps.detail: The adjustments are small and locally finite, so they converge on each compact set. The union of the triangulations of $U_1\subset U_2\subset\cdots$ is a locally finite [simplicial complex](c:simplicial-complex) homeomorphic to $M$.

concepts.c:manifold: The theorem says that low-dimensional manifolds are built from simplices.
concepts.c:triangulation: A triangulation is the simplicial structure that the proof builds.
concepts.c:simplicial-complex: The target is a locally finite simplicial complex.
concepts.c:surface: In dimension 2 the manifolds are surfaces, handled by Radó's argument.
concepts.c:3-manifold: In dimension 3 the argument relies on tame approximation in 3-manifolds.

source.ref: E. E. Moise, Affine structures in 3-manifolds. V. The triangulation theorem and Hauptvermutung, Annals of Mathematics 56 (1952), 96-114; for dimension 2, T. Radó, Über den Begriff der Riemannschen Fläche, Acta Litterarum ac Scientiarum Szeged 2 (1925), 101-121
source.note: Moise's paper proves dimension 3; Radó's paper proves dimension 2.

statement: Let $X$ and $Y$ be spaces with $Y$ [compact](c:compact-space), let $x\in X$, and let $N$ be an [open](c:open-set) subset of $X\times Y$ with $\{x\}\times Y\subseteq N$. Then some open $U\ni x$ has $U\times Y\subseteq N$.

hypotheses.text: The space $Y$ is [compact](c:compact-space).
The set $N$ is [open](c:open-set) in the [product topology](c:product-topology) of $X\times Y$ and contains $\{x\}\times Y$.

conclusion: There is an [open](c:open-set) set $U\ni x$ in $X$ with $U\times Y\subseteq N$.

proofs.name: Finite subcover of the slice
proofs.slogan: Cover the slice $\{x\}\times Y$ by basic boxes inside $N$, keep finitely many, and intersect their $X$-sides.
proofs.scope: All topological spaces $X$ and compact $Y$. If $Y=\emptyset$, then $U=X$ works, and the proof covers this case by an empty intersection.

roles.why: Openness of $N$ in the product topology gives a basic box around each point of the slice.
Compactness of $Y$ keeps finitely many boxes, so the intersection of their $X$-sides is open.

steps.slogan: Cover the slice by basic open boxes that lie inside $N$.
steps.detail: For each $y\in Y$, the point $(x,y)$ lies in the open set $N$. So there are open sets $U_y\ni x$ and $V_y\ni y$ with $U_y\times V_y\subseteq N$. The sets $V_y$ form an [open cover](c:open-cover) of $Y$.

steps.slogan: Select a finite subcover $V_{y_1},\dots,V_{y_k}$ of $Y$.
steps.detail: Because $Y$ is [compact](c:compact-space), finitely many of the sets $V_y$ cover $Y$. This finiteness is derived here; it is not a hypothesis.

steps.slogan: Intersect the finitely many $X$-sides to get one open neighborhood of $x$.
steps.detail: Put $U=U_{y_1}\cap\dots\cap U_{y_k}$. A finite intersection of [open sets](c:open-set) is open, and $x\in U$. If $k=0$, then $Y=\emptyset$ and $U=X$.

steps.slogan: Check that the tube $U	imes Y$ lies inside $N$.
steps.detail: Take $(a,b)\in U\times Y$. Some $V_{y_i}$ contains $b$, and $a\in U\subseteq U_{y_i}$. So $(a,b)\in U_{y_i}\times V_{y_i}\subseteq N$.

concepts.c:compact-space: Compactness of $Y$ reduces the cover of the slice to a finite one.
concepts.c:open-set: Open sets give the boxes and make the finite intersection open.
concepts.c:product-topology: Basic boxes are the basic open sets of the product topology.
concepts.c:open-cover: The $Y$-sides of the boxes form the cover that compactness reduces.

source.note: The standard proof of the tube lemma (Munkres, Topology, Lemma 26.8).

statement: Let $G$ be a [topological group](c:topological-group) with a right-invariant measure $\mu$, $\Gamma\le G$ a countable subgroup, and $\mathcal F$ a [fundamental domain](c:fundamental-domain) for $\Gamma$. If $f$ is $\mu$-integrable and its automorphization $f^\Gamma(x\Gamma)=\sum_{\gamma\in\Gamma}f(x\gamma)$ is measurable, then $\int_Gf\,d\mu=\int_{G/\Gamma}f^\Gamma\,d\mu_{\mathcal F}$, where $\mu_{\mathcal F}$ is the image of $\mu|_{\mathcal F}$ in the [quotient](c:quotient-group) $G/\Gamma$.

hypotheses.text: $G$ is a [topological group](c:topological-group) with its Borel $\sigma$-algebra, and $\mu$ is a right-invariant measure on $G$.
The [subgroup](c:subgroup) $\Gamma\le G$ is countable.
The measurable set $\mathcal F$ is a [fundamental domain](c:fundamental-domain) for the right action of $\Gamma$: its translates cover $G$ and overlap in null sets.
The function $f\colon G\to E$ is [integrable](c:integrable-function) for $\mu$, with values in a real Banach space $E$.
The automorphization $f^\Gamma$ is almost everywhere strongly measurable for $\mu_{\mathcal F}$.

formal.difference: The declaration is the additive version, and QuotientGroup.integral_eq_integral_automorphize is its multiplicative twin. It takes values in any real normed space, whereas this statement uses a real Banach space.

proofs.name: Unfold over the fundamental domain
proofs.slogan: Cut the group into translates of the fundamental domain, swap the sum and the integral, and push forward to the quotient.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, with $\mathcal F$ and $\Gamma$ as stated. The sum over $\Gamma$ converges absolutely for almost every $x\in\mathcal F$, because $f$ is integrable.

roles.why: Right invariance of $\mu$ moves each translate of $\mathcal F$ back to $\mathcal F$, and the quotient map is continuous.
A countable $\Gamma$ makes the decomposition a countable sum and allows the swap.
The fundamental domain splits $G$ into almost disjoint translates that cover $G$.
Integrability gives absolute convergence of the sum and the swap of sum and integral.
Measurability of $f^\Gamma$ lets the integral over $\mathcal F$ be pushed to the quotient.

steps.slogan: Cut $G$ into the translates $\mathcal F\gamma$ of the fundamental domain.
steps.detail: The translates cover $G$ and overlap in null sets, and $\Gamma$ is countable. So countable additivity of the integral of the integrable $f$ gives $\int_Gf\,d\mu=\sum_{\gamma\in\Gamma}\int_{\mathcal F\gamma}f\,d\mu$.

steps.slogan: Move each piece back to $\mathcal F$ by right translation.
steps.detail: Right invariance of $\mu$ gives $\int_{\mathcal F\gamma}f\,d\mu=\int_{\mathcal F}f(x\gamma)\,d\mu(x)$. Hence $\int_Gf\,d\mu=\sum_\gamma\int_{\mathcal F}f(x\gamma)\,d\mu(x)$.

steps.slogan: Swap the sum over $\Gamma$ and the integral over $\mathcal F$.
steps.detail: The same cutting for $\|f\|$ gives $\sum_\gamma\int_{\mathcal F}\|f(x\gamma)\|\,d\mu=\int_G\|f\|\,d\mu<\infty$. By the Tonelli and Fubini theorems for series, $\sum_\gamma\int_{\mathcal F}f(x\gamma)\,d\mu=\int_{\mathcal F}\sum_\gamma f(x\gamma)\,d\mu$.

steps.slogan: Push the integral over $\mathcal F$ forward to the quotient.
steps.detail: The sum $\sum_\gamma f(x\gamma)$ is $f^\Gamma(x\Gamma)$. For the measurable quotient map $\pi\colon G\to G/\Gamma$, change of variables gives $\int_{\mathcal F}f^\Gamma(\pi x)\,d\mu=\int_{G/\Gamma}f^\Gamma\,d\mu_{\mathcal F}$. This step needs the measurability of $f^\Gamma$.

concepts.c:topological-group: Group translations are measure preserving, and the quotient map is continuous.
concepts.c:subgroup: The subgroup $\Gamma$ indexes the translates and the sum.
concepts.c:fundamental-domain: The fundamental domain makes the translates cover $G$ once.
concepts.c:integrable-function: Integrability gives absolutely convergent sums and justifies the swap.
concepts.c:quotient-group: The integral over the quotient is the folded integral over $G$.

source.note: mathlib cuts G along the translates of the domain (IsAddFundamentalDomain.integral_eq_tsum''), swaps sum and integral with integral_tsum, and pushes forward with integral_map.
